title: CAN CHRISTIANS REALLY EAT ANYTHING—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT FOOD?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS REALLY EAT ANYTHING—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT FOOD?

Jesus spoke about what defiles a person. Peter saw a sheet descend from heaven. Paul said nothing is unclean in itself. Yet Leviticus still sits in our Bible, calling some animals clean and others unclean. So what actually changed—and what didn't?
There is a strange kind of tension that can happen at a Christian dinner table.
Someone bows his head and thanks God for the meal.
Someone else looks at what is on the plate and quietly wonders...
Can a Christian actually eat that?
Then come the questions.
Didn't God forbid certain animals?
Didn't Jesus say all foods were clean?
Didn't Peter refuse to eat unclean animals even after Christ's resurrection?
What about pork?
Shellfish?
Blood?
Food sacrificed to idols?
Were the food laws abolished, fulfilled, transformed, or simply ignored by modern Christians?
And beneath all those questions is a much deeper one.
When I open my Bible, am I willing to let Scripture correct me—even when it corrects something I have believed for years?
Because this isn't really an argument about bacon.
It is an argument about how we read the Bible.
And somewhere between Leviticus and the dinner table, Christians have sometimes made two opposite mistakes.
One side can turn dietary observance into a measuring stick for righteousness.
The other can speak as though the Old Testament was God's embarrassing first draft.
Both miss something beautiful.
Because Jesus did not come to rescue us from a defective God.
The God who spoke through Moses is the God revealed perfectly in Christ.
So we have to begin where Scripture begins.
God really did give Israel food laws.
Not imaginary laws.
Not suggestions.
Not merely ancient nutrition advice.
Actual covenant commands.
Leviticus 11 distinguishes between animals Israel could eat and animals Israel could not eat. Near the chapter's conclusion, the Hebrew says:
לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַטָּמֵא וּבֵין הַטָּהֹר
lehavdil bein hattame uvein hattahor
"...to distinguish between the unclean and the clean..."
The two important Hebrew ideas are טָמֵא — tame, "unclean," and טָהוֹר — tahor, "clean."
Leviticus 11:47 goes on to distinguish "between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten."
We should not erase that.
God gave those distinctions to Israel within the Mosaic covenant.
They were real.
They mattered.
They taught God's covenant people that holiness reached into ordinary life.
Their worship mattered.
Their bodies mattered.
Their tables mattered.
What they touched mattered.
What they ate mattered.
God was teaching a people rescued from slavery that belonging to Him was not something confined to a religious ceremony.
Holiness followed them home.
It entered their kitchens.
It sat beside them at dinner.
And maybe that is the first conviction modern Christians need to recover.
We can become so eager to defend Christian liberty that we forget liberty was never permission to stop caring about holiness.
But then Jesus comes.
And something enormous happens.
In Mark 7, Jesus is confronting controversy surrounding ritual defilement. His focus is not a casual debate over someone's favorite meal. He drives the discussion toward the human heart.
The surviving Greek text contains this striking phrase:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
katharizōn panta ta brōmata
Literally, the wording carries the sense of "cleansing all foods."

That is why many modern translations render Mark 7:19 along the lines of Jesus declaring all foods clean. The immediate context is Jesus explaining that what enters a person from outside does not penetrate the heart and therefore is not what morally defiles the person.
Then Jesus turns the knife toward the place we would rather avoid.
The heart.
Because what comes from within?
Sexual immorality.
Theft.
Murder.
Adultery.
Greed.
Wickedness.
Deceit.
Sensuality.
Envy.
Slander.
Pride.
Foolishness.
Suddenly the person obsessing over another believer's plate has nowhere to hide.
You can inspect every ingredient...
and still have a filthy heart.
You can refuse pork while consuming pornography.
You can inspect food labels while feeding hatred.
You can meticulously avoid shellfish while devouring another person's reputation through gossip.
You can have a religiously impressive kitchen and an unrepentant soul.
And Jesus keeps dragging the conversation back to the place religious people often desperately try to escape.
The heart.
That does not mean God's earlier commands were evil.
It means those commands belonged within a covenantal story that was moving toward Christ.
And then we arrive at Peter.
Acts 10.
Peter is hungry.
He falls into a trance.
Something resembling a great sheet descends containing various animals.
A voice tells him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter recoils.
He says he has never eaten anything common or unclean.
That detail matters.
This is after Jesus' resurrection.
Peter's instincts had not simply disappeared overnight.
But then comes the voice:
Ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν σὺ μὴ κοίνου.
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
"What God has cleansed, you must not call common."
But here we need to be careful.
Acts itself tells us that Peter's vision is profoundly about people, particularly the inclusion of Gentiles.
Peter later explains the lesson: God showed him that he should not call any person common or unclean.
So it would be careless to reduce Acts 10 to: "Peter learned he could finally eat pork."
The vision is much bigger than Peter's lunch.
Cornelius is coming.
The Gentiles are coming.
People once regarded as outside are being brought near through Christ.
God is dismantling the barriers that would prevent Jewish believers from receiving Gentile believers as members of God's redeemed people.
The sheet is not merely about a menu.
It is about a mission.
It is about the Gospel crossing boundaries.
It is about grace walking through a Gentile doorway.
And that becomes even clearer in Acts 15.
A crisis erupts in the early Church.
Gentiles are believing in Jesus.
So the explosive question becomes:
Must these Gentile believers effectively come under the Mosaic covenant in order to belong to God's people?
The apostles gather.
They debate.
They listen.
They search what God is doing.
And the resulting apostolic letter does something incredibly important.
It does not impose the whole Mosaic law upon Gentile converts.

Acts 15:28–29 says that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and the apostles not to place a greater burden upon them beyond several requirements: abstaining from things sacrificed to idols, blood, what had been strangled, and sexual immorality.
Whatever debates Christians may have about every detail of those instructions, one fact is difficult to escape:
The apostles had the perfect opportunity to tell Gentile believers, "You must now observe the complete Levitical dietary code."
They did not do that.
And then Paul becomes even more explicit.
Romans 14 deals with believers whose consciences differed over food and sacred days.
And listen carefully to Paul's Greek:
οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι’ ἑαυτοῦ
Oida kai pepeismai en Kyriō Iēsou hoti ouden koinon di' heautou.
"I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself..."
Paul does not say this hesitantly.
He anchors his conviction "in the Lord Jesus."
Yet he immediately protects the conscience of the believer who considers something unclean.
That changes the atmosphere completely.
Christian freedom is real.
But Christian freedom is not selfish.
Paul will not allow the strict believer to condemn the free believer.
And he will not allow the free believer to despise the strict believer.
Read that again.
Because churches have been wounded over things smaller than dinner.
One Christian says, "I don't eat pork because I believe abstaining honors God."
Another says, "I receive it with thanksgiving because I believe I am free in Christ."
Paul's instinct is not:
"Excellent. Destroy each other."
It is almost the opposite.
Stop despising one another.
Stop passing judgment over disputable matters.
Walk in love.
Do not destroy your brother over food.
Because the kingdom of God is bigger than your plate.
This is where Christian maturity becomes painfully practical.
You may possess freedom...
and still choose restraint because you love someone.
You may possess a conviction...
and still refuse to turn that conviction into a throne from which you judge everyone else.
That is Gospel maturity.
And Paul does not stop there.
Writing to Timothy, he warns about people who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving.
Then comes another remarkable Greek statement:
ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ καλόν, καὶ οὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον μετὰ εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον
hoti pan ktisma Theou kalon, kai ouden apoblēton meta eucharistias lambanomenon
"For every creation of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when received with thanksgiving."
And now the biblical trajectory becomes difficult to miss.
Leviticus genuinely distinguishes clean and unclean animals for Israel.
Jesus redirects the question of defilement toward the heart and Mark records the striking language concerning the cleansing of foods.
Peter's vision uses clean/unclean categories while God prepares him to welcome Gentiles.
The Jerusalem Council refuses to place the full Mosaic yoke upon Gentile converts.
Paul says nothing is unclean in itself.
Paul tells Timothy that God's creation may be received with thanksgiving.
And Colossians tells believers not to allow others to sit in judgment over them regarding food, drink, festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths.
So...
Can Christians eat anything?

In terms of the Levitical clean-versus-unclean animal classifications as covenant obligations, the New Testament does not place Gentile Christians under Israel's complete dietary code as a requirement for belonging to God.
But that does not mean the Christian position is simply:
"Eat anything. Nothing matters."
Because Paul gives us a far more demanding principle.
"Whether you eat or drink...do all to the glory of God."
Do you see what happened?
The question changed.
Not merely:
"Am I technically allowed to eat this?"
But:
"Can I glorify Jesus in this?"
That is harder.
Because legalism loves minimum requirements.
Love asks deeper questions.
Is this wise for my body?
Am I enslaved by appetite?
Am I eating with gratitude?
Am I knowingly participating in idolatry?
Am I violating my conscience?
Am I wounding someone else's conscience merely to prove that I am free?
Is food controlling me?
Am I turning my personal conviction into a righteousness test God never commanded for the Church?
Am I judging someone Christ has received?
Those questions reach far beyond pork.
They reach into gluttony.
Addiction.
Vanity.
Self-control.
Hospitality.
Poverty.
Gratitude.
Fellowship.
Conscience.
Love.
And worship.
Because Christianity was never supposed to create people who obsess over religious boundaries while ignoring the condition of their souls.
Imagine standing before Jesus saying:
"Lord, I never ate the wrong animal."
But you never forgave your brother.
You hated your neighbor.
You secretly fed lust.
You worshiped money.
You crushed weaker believers with your pride.
You knew biblical terminology but never surrendered your heart.
That is precisely why Jesus' words in Mark 7 cut so deeply.
The most dangerous thing on your table may not be what is on your plate.
It may be what is sitting inside your heart.
And maybe this debate has become personal for you.
Maybe you grew up being told that eating certain foods could separate you from God.
Maybe you were taught that Christians who eat pork are disobedient.
Maybe you came from the opposite direction and were taught to mock believers who still abstain.
Maybe you've spent years frightened that one mistake could make you spiritually unclean.
Hear the Gospel.
Your justification before God does not come from your menu.
It comes through Jesus Christ.
You cannot diet your way into forgiveness.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by avoiding enough ingredients.
You cannot earn the cross.
Jesus did not bleed because your dietary discipline was almost sufficient.
He bled because it never could be.
Sin goes deeper than the stomach.
It reaches the heart.
And therefore salvation had to go deeper too.
Jesus carried sin.
Jesus bore judgment.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus welcomes sinners who repent and trust Him.
And when He saves us, He does not merely hand us permission slips.
He gives us Himself.
That means Christian liberty should never make us arrogant.
And personal conviction should never make us self-righteous.
If you abstain from certain foods as a personal act of conscience before God, you do not need to be mocked.
Honor Christ.
Give thanks.
Remain humble.
If you eat foods another Christian abstains from, you do not need to feel spiritually inferior merely because another believer's conscience differs.
Honor Christ.
Give thanks.
Remain humble.
But neither person gets to replace Jesus with a plate.
The stricter Christian is not saved by abstinence.
The freer Christian is not spiritually mature merely because he exercises liberty.
Christ is the center.
And perhaps that is what this entire controversy has been trying to expose.
We humans desperately want something measurable.
Something visible.
Something we can point toward and say:
"See? I am one of the faithful ones."
But Jesus keeps pointing toward the heart.
Pride is harder to photograph than pork.
Bitterness has no nutrition label.
Lust doesn't appear on an ingredient list.
Greed isn't printed beside the calories.
Unforgiveness has no warning sticker.
Self-righteousness can sit at a perfectly biblical-looking table.
And still be starving for grace.
That is the scandal.
The person eating the "right" food can still desperately need Jesus.
The person eating the "wrong" food can still desperately need Jesus.
The religious person needs Jesus.
The rebellious person needs Jesus.
The disciplined need Jesus.
The addicted need Jesus.
The person who has memorized Leviticus needs Jesus.
The person who has never opened Leviticus needs Jesus.
All roads eventually lead us to the same humiliating and beautiful confession:
I cannot save myself.
And that is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Jesus does not merely rewrite your menu.
Jesus rewrites you.
He takes people obsessed with external purity and teaches them purity of heart.
He takes people abusing freedom and teaches them love.
He takes frightened consciences and teaches them grace.
He takes proud consciences and teaches them humility.
He takes divided tables and creates a family.
So before your next argument about food...
look across the table.
That believer belongs to Someone.
If Christ received them, be very careful before making food the test by which you reject them.
Be honest before Jesus.
Not to start another war. Tell us what Scripture taught you, what you once believed, what changed, or where you are still struggling.
Someone reading your testimony may realize they are not alone.
Come back to it with your Bible open.
Read Leviticus 11.
Read Mark 7.
Read Acts 10.
Read Acts 15.
Read Romans 14.
Read 1 Corinthians 8–10.
Read Colossians 2.
Read 1 Timothy 4.
Don't build your theology from a meme.
Don't build it from one isolated verse.
And don't build it from this article alone.
Go back to the Word.

And whether you support financially or cannot give anything at all, you can still help.
Pray.

Because ministry was never supposed to terminate with the person who received the truth.
Truth travels.
Grace travels.
Testimony travels.
The Gospel travels.
And maybe tonight the question you thought was about food has uncovered something far more important.
You came asking:
"What am I allowed to eat?"
But Jesus may be asking:
"What has been eating your heart?"
Pride?
Fear?
Legalism?
Shame?
Religious superiority?
Secret sin?
A desperate attempt to make yourself clean enough for God?
Bring it to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
Then get up and walk with Him.
Because the greatest miracle at the Christian table is not that certain foods can be eaten.
It is that sinners who had no right to sit at the King's table have been invited near through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And when grace finally reaches the heart, you discover that the most important thing Jesus wanted to cleanse was never your plate—it was you.
